materials.text: Pattern-making and sewing combine material choices, tools and experienced skill; reconstructed garments document research rather than original manufacture.

knowledge.text: Changing materials can accompany continuing community identity and knowledge.

custody.text: The named historical photograph and community-led reconstruction answer different questions.

name: Inuinnait clothing: skill, identity and change
place: Coronation Gulf and Victoria Island region, Canadian Arctic
geographicPrecision: Broad regional locator for the expedition context, not an exact exposure site or the boundary of all Inuit homelands.

interval.label: Selected expedition context, 1913–1916
interval.note: This is the Southern Party observation window named in Jenness’s 1922 report, not the lifespan of Inuinnait clothing or peoples. The photograph is individually undated and was published in 1922. Later community research interprets this history without extending the selected interval.

question: How does clothing carry practical knowledge and identity through change?
summary: Making clothes connected seasonal harvesting, prepared materials, skilled hands and relationships. A named expedition photograph shows two people in dancing costume; community-directed research explains practical work and change that the image alone cannot recover.

sections.title: Work begins before a seam
sections.text: The community’s Patterns of Change exhibit connects clothing to seasonal life: sealing on winter sea ice and smaller summer groups harvesting caribou and fish. Its 1880s account names copper and bone needles, caribou sinew thread, and caribou and seal skins. Materials had to become usable clothing through work. The public drum-dancing guide describes scraping, drying, cleaning and softening skins before sewing. A garment therefore joins harvesting and preparation with the experienced decisions of its maker; its finished pattern is only part of that work.

sections.title: Clothes suited to an activity
sections.text: The same guide distinguishes thick travelling clothes from lighter garments suited to dancing. It links late-summer caribou hides with the lightness and softness wanted for dance clothing. In the historical photograph, contrasting bands, different hood shapes and hanging details are visible. The caption names Ikpakhuak and Higilak in dancing costume. These particular clothes should not become a universal picture of daily Arctic work, and the photograph does not reveal who made each garment or which hide was used.

sections.title: New supplies changed the choices
sections.text: For its 1930s frame, PI/KHS describes cotton outer covers, duffle-wool linings and steel tools entering clothing work through exchange. Its 1950s account adds ready-made supplies and hand-crank sewing machines. Change also involved pressure: the community account describes government decisions about settlement, wage work and distant schooling where children were forbidden to practise their language and culture. Other families continued hunting and fishing in outpost camps. Access to new cloth was part of a changing social world, rather than proof that everyone freely chose the same transition.

citations.locator: English body: government decisions, outposts and clothing

sections.title: Makers research and teach
sections.text: Between 2017 and 2019, Elders Mary Avalak, Mabel Etegik and Annie Atighioyak guided community workshops researching five historical parkas. Participants prepared hides, made patterns and sewed garments using period-appropriate supplies. Language work accompanied the making, and learners were encouraged to use their knowledge for family and friends. The exhibit presents these as modern researched reconstructions. Its 2010s account emphasizes continuing making by Inuinnait, including new fabrics alongside familiar cuts and fur trim. Knowledge can be maintained through adaptation as well as careful reconstruction.

deeperReading.title: Keep the dates attached to the right evidence
deeperReading.text: The case interval remains 1913–16, the expedition’s selected Southern Party window. The complete printed plate was published in 1922; it gives no exact exposure date. An exhibit parka representing the 1880s is different again: community participants researched and made it in 2017–19. Those three clocks cannot be exchanged. Nor does the later guide’s general description of dance clothing prove the precise material, maker or preparation of each garment in the photograph. The source comparison explains plausible kinds of work while keeping the named image’s missing details visible.

deeperReading.title: Read makers through the source that offers their knowledge
deeperReading.text: The public guide profiles June Klengenberg as a seamstress sharing knowledge with grandchildren and her community; its photograph caption dates the pictured dance coat to a 2011 occasion. That account is not a new interview, proof of her present circumstances or testimony about the older plate. The exhibit’s named Elders likewise organize a particular teaching project, rather than standing for every Inuit community. Here their institution’s English explanations are used with attribution. No audio was transcribed, no independent Inuinnaqtun translation was made, and no pattern or ceremonial design was copied. Learning about work does not require claiming ownership of its designs.

evidenceReading.title: A photograph, a preparation account and a researched reconstruction
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases of selected sources. The named people, represented periods, publication dates and modern research dates remain distinct.

items.label: The complete printed plate
items.text: Plate I names Ikpakhuak and Higilak in dancing costume. The preserved page shows contrasting bands, two different hood shapes and hanging details.
items.interpretation: The visible garment features can be described without identifying every material, maker or symbolic meaning. The 1922 publication date does not settle the exposure date, and dancing costume is not every person’s daily outfit.

citations.locator: Actual full Plate I; archive publication metadata

items.label: Preparation and seasonal properties
items.text: The community-published guide describes preparing skins before sewing and connects late-summer hides with the lighter clothing wanted for dancing.
items.interpretation: This explains why preparation and timing matter to a maker. It does not establish the harvest season of each skin in the old photograph or supply a complete pattern for reproducing a ceremonial outfit.

items.label: Making an exhibit is also knowledge work
items.text: PI/KHS describes Elders-led workshops in 2017–19 researching period materials, preparing hides, making patterns, sewing parkas and documenting language.
items.interpretation: The resulting garments are modern researched reconstructions. They can show a process of learning without being mislabeled as originals made in the 1880s, 1930s or 1950s.

familyActivity.title: Follow a material and check its clock
steps: Look at the complete plate. Describe one difference between the two hoods and one contrasting band. Read the printed caption before deciding what kind of clothing is shown.

Read this capsule: the community exhibit’s 1880s account names copper/bone needles, sinew and skins; its 1930s account names cotton covers, wool linings and steel tools. Elders-led workshops in 2017–19 researched and sewed modern parkas representing earlier periods. The photograph was published in 1922 and its exact exposure is undated.

Choose one material/tool change from the capsule. Write what a maker would need to learn or obtain. Then sort “represented 1880s,” “published 1922” and “made in the workshops 2017–19” into three different evidence labels. Can the photograph alone prove your chosen change?
familyActivity.explanation: Cotton, wool or a steel needle would require access to those supplies and knowledge of how to use them; the capsule supplies that change. The photograph supports description of the visible clothes, rather than an entire account of production. A parka representing the 1880s can have been made in 2017–19. Publication in 1922 does not give the exposure’s exact date. No copied cultural design or reconstructed ceremony is needed for this comparison.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author checking; not independent historian, Inuinnait community or maker approval
review.scope: A bounded registry DEEPEN account of seasonal/material work, attributed community interpretation and teaching. The full original 1913–16 interval, identity, claims, comparison texts, coordinates, object order, plate metadata and both image files remain preserved. The broader selected reference does not extend the case interval.
limitations: The old photograph’s exact exposure date/location, individual photographer, garment makers, exact materials and wearer testimony remain unestablished. The complete plate and caption are retained; the image is not a universal Arctic outfit.

Community web publication dates and the selected drum-dancing guide’s edition date remain unknown. Its 2011 caption and older age wording do not establish current biography. Only selected English text was used; no original interviews, audio, independent Inuinnaqtun translation or complete cited historical sources were checked.

The community institution’s account of outside pressures and adaptation is attributed. It does not represent every household’s experience or substitute for a complete history of schooling, settlement, health or other Inuit peoples.

No new photograph, pattern, tracing, source-plan copy, annotation, cultural-design reproduction, numeric geography or route is supplied. Public pattern-library access is not converted into a blanket licence for all photographs or designs. Existing publication-based rights remain unchanged.
